content: Tobacco use is the primary cause of preventable diseases, disabilities, and deaths in the United States. Smoking damages multiple organs, including the heart, lungs, kidneys, stomach, and intestines, and is a major contributor to various cancers. Quitting smoking significantly reduces health risks: cardiovascular risks decrease, the risk of stroke drops to about half that of a nonsmoker within a few years, and the risks of cancers such as those of the mouth, throat, esophagus, and bladder are halved within five years. Ten years after quitting, the risk of lung cancer is reduced by half. Smoking cessation can be achieved through both non-pharmacological and pharmacological strategies. Epidemiology of Smoking Tobacco use accounts for over 480,000 deaths annually in the U.S., representing one in every five deaths. In 2015, approximately 15.1% of U.S. adults (36.5 million people) were current smokers, a decline from 20.9% in 2005. However, nearly 40 million adults and 4.7 million middle and high school students still use tobacco products, including e-cigarettes. Every day, over 3,800 youths under 18 years old smoke their first cigarette. Smoking-related diseases cost the U.S. nearly $170 billion annually in medical care. Smoking Prevalence by Demographics Gender: 16.7% of adult men and 13.6% of adult women smoke. Age: Smoking rates are highest among adults aged 25–44 years (17.7%) and lowest among those aged 65 years and older (8.4%). Race/Ethnicity: Smoking prevalence is highest among non-Hispanic American Indians/Alaska Natives (21.9%) and lowest among non-Hispanic Asians (7.0%). Education: Adults with a GED certificate have the highest smoking rates (34.1%), while those with graduate degrees have the lowest (3.6%). Socioeconomic Status: Smoking is more common among adults living below the poverty level (26.1%) compared to those living at or above the poverty level (13.9%). Geography: Smoking rates are highest in the Midwest (18.7%) and lowest in the West (12.4%). Disability: Adults with disabilities or limitations have higher smoking rates (21.5%) than those without (13.8%). Sexual Orientation: Smoking is more prevalent among lesbian, gay, or bisexual adults (20.6%) compared to heterosexual adults (14.9%). Health Impacts of Smoking Mortality Cigarette smoking is the leading preventable cause of death in the U.S., causing over 480,000 deaths annually. This accounts for nearly one in five deaths. Smoking increases the risk of death from all causes in both men and women. Over the past 50 years, the risk of dying from smoking-related causes has increased. Smoking is responsible for 80% of deaths from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Cardiovascular Disease Smoking significantly increases the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke, which are leading causes of death in the U.S. Even smoking fewer than five cigarettes per day can lead to early signs of cardiovascular disease. Smoking damages blood vessels, causing them to thicken and narrow, which can lead to blockages. These blockages may result in strokes or reduced blood flow to the legs and skin. Respiratory Disease Smoking damages the airways and alveoli in the lungs, leading to diseases such as COPD, emphysema, and chronic bronchitis. It is the primary cause of lung cancer. Smokers are 12–13 times more likely to die from COPD than nonsmokers. Tobacco smoke can also exacerbate asthma symptoms. Cancer Smoking is a major cause of cancer in various parts of the body, including the bladder, blood (acute myeloid leukemia), cervix, colon, rectum, esophagus, kidney, ureter, larynx, liver, oropharynx, pancreas, stomach, trachea, bronchus, and lung. Smoking also increases the risk of cancer-related deaths. If smoking were eliminated, one-third of cancer deaths in the U.S. could be prevented. Reproductive and Other Health Risks Smoking negatively affects nearly every organ in the body. In women, it can impair fertility and increase the risk of complications such as preterm delivery, stillbirth, low birth weight, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), ectopic pregnancy, and orofacial clefts in infants. In men, smoking can reduce sperm quality, leading to infertility and increased risks of birth defects and miscarriage. Smoking weakens bones, particularly in postmenopausal women, increasing the risk of fractures. It also damages teeth and gums, leading to tooth loss, and increases the risk of cataracts and age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Smoking is a cause of type 2 diabetes, with smokers having a 30–40% higher risk of developing the disease. It also contributes to inflammation, decreased immune function, and rheumatoid arthritis. Benefits of Smoking Cessation Quitting smoking has immediate and long-term health benefits: Within one year, the risk of a heart attack drops significantly. Within 2–5 years, the risk of stroke decreases to that of a nonsmoker. Within five years, the risks of cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, and bladder are halved. After ten years, the risk of lung cancer is reduced by half. Smoking Cessation Strategies General Principles The 5As framework is an evidence-based approach to smoking cessation in healthcare settings: 1. Ask about tobacco use. 2. Advise the patient to quit. 3. Assess readiness to quit. 4. Assist with quitting. 5. Arrange follow-up care. Pharmacological Interventions First-line pharmacotherapies include nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) in various forms (patch, gum, lozenge, nasal spray, inhaler), sustained-release bupropion hydrochloride, and varenicline. Second-line therapies, such as clonidine and nortriptyline, are also effective. Bupropion: Start with 150 mg daily for three days, then increase to 150 mg twice daily. Treatment lasts 7–12 weeks, with maintenance therapy up to six months. Common side effects include insomnia and dry mouth. Nicotine Gum: For those smoking 1–24 cigarettes/day, use 2 mg gum; for ≥25 cigarettes/day, use 4 mg gum. Up to 24 pieces can be used daily for up to 12 weeks. Side effects include mouth soreness and dyspepsia. Nicotine Inhaler: Use 6–16 cartridges daily for up to six months. Side effects include local irritation of the mouth and throat. Nicotine Lozenges: For those who smoke their first cigarette >30 minutes after waking, use 2 mg lozenges; for ≤30 minutes, use 4 mg lozenges. Use 4–20 lozenges daily for up to 12 weeks. Side effects include nausea and heartburn. Nicotine Nasal Spray: Use 8–40 doses daily for 3–6 months. Side effects include nasal irritation. Varenicline: Start with 0.5 mg daily for three days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days, followed by 1 mg twice daily. Treatment lasts 3–6 months. Side effects include nausea, sleep disturbances, vivid dreams, and depressed mood.
